text.insert: Authority reaches a sandbox through the same two-level structure the
authority contract

defines: the dispatch lease grants the run workflow the right to dispatch worker agents and mutate its allowed checkout surfaces, and each target claim is the per-target worker ownership record created under that lease. The sandbox binds one-to-one to the claim and adds no third authority layer: it is capacity that executes fenced commands, never an actor that issues them.

props.title: Decision (2026-08-13) — sandbox lifetime is bound to the target claim

text.insert: A sandbox is created with its target claim, lives exactly as long as the claim is active, and is deleted when the claim settles or is cancelled. Sandbox lifecycle maps onto the claim's TTL and deadline layer rather than defining a parallel mechanism.

props.title: Decision (2026-08-13) — on-demand creation, stop-while-thinking, no warm pool

text.insert: Sandboxes are created on demand from the game image at claim creation and stopped while the model thinks. Warm pools are rejected: their claim restrictions exclude per-claim configuration, and idle running sandboxes bill compute and hold quota against an hour-scale worker lifecycle where creation latency is noise.
How the Lease Reaches Sandbox Execution
The lease is enforced by fencing, not trust: every worker-dispatch and source-mutation command presents the current
lease_id
, and a stale actor from a previous activation is refused rather than obeyed. Sandboxes fit that rule as follows:

The host worker process is the presenting actor — it holds the claim, presents the current lease id on every guarded command, and drives the sandbox as its execution surface; the sandbox itself never issues commands against harness state.
Every sandbox carries its binding as labels at creation, so any reconciler can map a live sandbox to the claim and lease acquisition that justify it without consulting process memory.
A sandbox whose labeled lease id is no longer current is an orphan: it holds no authority to refuse, so recovery deletes it rather than fencing it.

props.description: Labels stamped on every sandbox at creation; the platform-side record binding it to harness state.

fields.name: claim_id
fields.description: The target claim this sandbox executes for; exactly one sandbox per active claim.

fields.name: lease_id
fields.description: The dispatch-lease acquisition the claim was created under; a mismatch with the current lease marks the sandbox an orphan.

fields.name: trace_id
fields.description: Root trace of the worker state; ties sandbox operations into the tracing fabric.

props.name: SandboxLabels

text.insert: Reaping in Recovery and at Startup
Run recovery settles or cancels orphaned claims and breaks a stale dispatch lease when one is still held; sandbox reaping joins those existing steps instead of adding new ones:
Each cancelled claim id in
run.recovered
names exactly one sandbox to delete; deletion is part of settling that claim.

Startup reconciliation, which already reconciles pending integration rows before acquiring dispatch authority, additionally lists sandboxes by label and deletes any whose claim is closed or whose lease id does not match the current acquisition.
The platform TTL is the backstop beneath both: every sandbox is created with a wall-clock TTL set past the claim deadline, so a sandbox that recovery never reaches destroys itself.

props.title: Open call — guardian reaping of remote capacity

text.insert: Process guardians recover expired claims for broader process incidents but have no remote-resource step. Extending the guardian playbook with a sandbox sweep is deferred to the guardian pages; the label scheme above is sufficient evidence for it.
Stop While Thinking
A worker spends minutes of reasoning between tool-call bursts, and the host worker process — the actor awaiting the model — knows precisely when the sandbox is needed:

steps.text: A tool call arrives: start the sandbox if stopped, execute, return output
The model goes quiet: after roughly sixty to ninety seconds without calls, stop the sandbox
not instantly — calls cluster (edit, build, score), and a wake delay inside a cluster is a real cost
The claim settles or is cancelled: delete the sandbox

text.insert: A stopped sandbox bills disk only, releases its vCPU and memory back to the platform quota, and preserves the workspace on the runner for a fast wake — agent edits and incremental build state included.
Container stop does not preserve running processes, so long-lived background work must complete before a stop; tool calls are discrete commands, which is what makes the pattern safe.
The platform's inactivity auto-stop is disabled in favor of these explicit stops: its idle heuristic can misfire on long silent builds, and the TTL already backstops abandonment.
